title: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1–18)
hookLine: the people sing; the rabbis say God hushed the angels because the Egyptians were drowning (Megillah 10b)

lines: A TEST RESULT THAT COMES BACK CLEAR.
A PEOPLE ON A BEACH AT DAWN.
cards: A test result that comes back clear. A phone call saying they're safe. The moment the thing chasing you is gone.

Now multiply that relief by a whole people, standing on a beach at dawn, soaking wet, looking back at the water where the army was. Generations of slavery, and it's over. What do you do in a moment like that?
They sing. And the angels aren't allowed to join in.

teach.h: I WILL SING UNTO THE LORD.
teach.b: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD." It begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea."
This is Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea. In a Torah scroll it's even written differently from the text around it, laid out like bricks in a wall.
One line from it, "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?", in Hebrew mi chamocha, is said in Jewish prayer every single day. Nobody tells the people they were wrong to sing.
But the Talmud tells a story about that same moment.

Up in heaven, the ministering angels wanted to sing too, and God stopped them. The works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you want to sing? The Egyptians had enslaved and chased the Israelites.
They were still God's creatures. The Talmud adds a subtle line: God doesn't rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, though God may let others rejoice. The people who were just saved can sing.
But nobody should throw a party over someone drowning.

teach.h: A DROP OF WINE FOR EACH PLAGUE.
teach.b: In the same spirit, at the seder, many people spill a drop of wine for each of the ten plagues. One explanation: a full cup is a sign of joy, and the joy is made a little less, because people suffered.

teach.h: REJOICE NOT WHEN THINE ENEMY FALLETH.
teach.b: The book of Proverbs says it too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." Be grateful you're safe. Sing.
Just don't sing over the drowning.

how: Jews say the Song of the Sea in the morning prayers, and its line mi chamocha in the evening and morning prayers; at the seder many spill a drop of wine for each plague, and the Song is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover.

o: a victory chant sung over a fallen enemy
who is like You, a line from the Song said daily
the brick-like way the Song is laid out

games.q: what's inside the song — tap the pairs.
p: joy made smaller at the seder

s: the Talmud says the Israelites were wrong to sing
the story is about the angels. the people who were saved sang, and the song is said every day.
the Song of the Sea is written differently in a Torah scroll
it's laid out in a pattern like bricks in a wall.
at the seder, wine is spilled to add to the celebration
a drop is removed for each plague, so the cup of joy is less full.

games.q: you're one of the angels. the people below are singing on the shore. you want to sing too. what does the Talmud say happened?
o: God stopped them: my creatures are drowning.
the angels sang a sad song instead.
games.why: God said: the works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you would sing? the people's thanks stands; the angels stay silent.

practice: Think of a recent win, something that went your way: an argument, a game, a promotion, a rival who stumbled, and let yourself be really glad about it.
Then think of the person on the other side and what it cost them, and hold both at once. If you pray, you can give thanks for what went well.

wordCard.voice: Mi chamocha, Hebrew for who is like You: a line from the Song said in Jewish prayer every day, sung on the far shore while the angels were told to be quiet.

orig.note: Hebrew: who is like You? a line from the Song, said in Jewish prayer every day.

carryVoice: Your line: don't sing over the drowning. Gratitude can sing without gloating. See you tomorrow.
